body: Core practices: (1) Inversion - before buying, list how the investment could fail (pre-mortem) and avoid those paths; 'all I want to know is where I'm going to die, so I'll never go there.' (2) Latticework - check a thesis with models from several disciplines: incentives, scale economics, network effects, compounding, opportunity cost, regression to the mean. (3) A bias checklist from 'The Psychology of Human Misjudgment' (1995): incentive-caused bias, social proof, commitment/consistency, deprival super-reaction, envy, denial, authority, and 'lollapalooza' when several combine (e.g., Indian IPO/SME manias). (4) Few great bets, held long; 'the big money is not in the buying and selling but in the waiting.' (5) Quality over cheapness: wonderful business at a fair price. Evidence: Munger's own partnership showed -30%+ years in 1973-74, so concentration requires capacity to endure drawdowns. Individual use: a written one-page pre-mortem and bias check per stock.
title: Munger: inversion, mental-model latticework, and sitting still

body: Rules (from his interviews): (1) Keep a sector avoid list - industries with chronically poor shareholder returns or governance (he has named PSUs, commodities, utilities, real estate among them at various times); excluding them cuts the error rate. (2) Diversify across ~30-40 growth stocks rather than a few bets. (3) Sell losers when the thesis is wrong instead of averaging down - he argues fewer than 5% of stocks are worth holding for the real long term, so long holding by itself is not an edge. (4) Let winners run. (5) Use macro judgment occasionally (raising cash in crises). Trade-off: avoid lists miss sector-wide rerating rallies (e.g., Indian PSUs 2021-24) - the cost of insurance against blow-ups. For an individual: write the avoid list down, define a review trigger for any stock down 25-30% from cost (re-underwrite, don't auto-average), and cap position size.
title: Samir Arora: avoid-list plus cut-losers discipline
